The reader knows there are three riders, and "her companion" could refer to either Tom or the unnamed man. But looking again: the sentence reads "He wanted to go and didn't see her companion had determined he shouldn't." However, the draft does say "they were three on horseback—Tom, another man, and a pretty woman," so "her companion" most naturally reads as the unnamed man (not Tom), since Tom is separately named. A competent reader would infer this. This is borderline but I think the reader is not genuinely confused — they'd understand "the other horseman." Not a finding.

**Ch 007 draft checks:**

He had found George Wilson sick in his office that afternoon..." The source says he strolled over "after five" and found Wilson. The draft says "that afternoon" — fine. Then: "A little after seven, Mrs. Wilson's voice could be heard, loud and scolding, downstairs in the garage." The draft removes this — Michaelis simply disappears as a named presence after the Wilson dialogue, and then "A little after seven, Mrs. Wilson's voice could be heard" arrives without an observer. - "Some words from the policeman's questioning reached Wilson" — in the draft, the extended policeman-Michaelis exchange naming the yellow car was cut, but the draft does include Tom's earlier denial about the yellow car, so Wilson's response "You don't have to tell me what kind of car it was! I know what kind of car it was!" has a logical antecedent (the policeman is questioning witnesses, and Wilson hears something). However, the draft doesn't show any policeman questioning before this moment in the garage scene. Looking at the draft garage scene: Tom pushes through, Myrtle's body is described, Wilson is described, then "Some words from the policeman's questioning reached Wilson." The policeman has not been introduced in the draft's garage scene at all — no policeman has appeared yet in the draft at this point. The source had "a motorcycle policeman taking down names" introduced in the same paragraph as the body. The draft omitted this. So "the policeman's questioning" refers to a policeman not yet established in the draft at that point in the scene.

Let me recheck: The draft says: "Myrtle Wilson's body, wrapped in a blanket...lay on a worktable by the wall. Wilson stood on the raised threshold of his office..." — no policeman mentioned. Then: "Some words from the policeman's questioning reached Wilson, and suddenly a new theme found voice..." — this is a dangling definite reference. A reader has not been told a policeman is present. Then later: "The policeman caught something in the tone and looked over. 'And what colour's your car?'" — the policeman speaks here. So the policeman is first mentioned as "the policeman" in "Some words from the policeman's questioning" before being introduced. This is a genuine mid-scene definite reference with no antecedent in the draft.

This is a real finding: "Some words from the policeman's questioning reached Wilson" uses a definite article for a policeman never introduced in the draft's garage scene.

- "So we drove on toward death through the cooling twilight." — This sentence closes the thirty/birthday section. It's a narrative transition that works as an ominous foreshadowing. The reader understands the car is heading toward what will be a death scene. Not genuinely confusing.

- "Tom came out of the house wrapping a quart bottle in a towel, followed by Daisy and Jordan in small tight hats of metallic cloth." — The source has them carrying "light capes over their arms." The draft omits this detail but the sentence parses fine. Not a finding.

- "'Did you see that?' demanded Tom." followed immediately by "He looked at me keenly, realizing that Jordan and I must have known all along." — In the source, between these two sentences Tom says "See what?" / "He looked at me keenly." The draft cuts the "See what?" exchange. So Tom demands "Did you see that?" and then without any reply, the next sentence is "He looked at me keenly, realizing that Jordan and I must have known all along." This is slightly abrupt but the reader can infer that no one answered, or that Tom read their silence. The source's "See what?" / "He looked at me keenly" is just Nick's non-reply rendered as a beat. A competent reader would not be confused. Not a finding.

- In the draft: "I wanted to get up and slap him on the back. The draft has prior context of Nick's relationship with Gatsby, and the phrasing "renewals...that I'd experienced before" is self-explanatory. Not a finding.

- The draft Ch 007 opens: "It was when curiosity about Gatsby was at its highest that the lights in his house failed to go on one Saturday night—and, as obscurely as it had begun, his career as Trimalchio was over." — "Trimalchio" is a reference that appears here without any prior gloss in either draft chapter. The source also uses it here without gloss (it's the source's first use of the term too). So this isn't something cut from the draft — the source itself doesn't gloss it in this chapter. Not a finding attributable to compression.
